raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    The graph demonstrates the number of books being banned in the US by state. At first glance, I noticed that Florida has the most books prohibited due to the darkness of the color of the state. I was also able to tell that some states have not banned any books during this period. The states with the most books banned are very spread out and not all in the same region. I was also surprised at how many states have banned books since I don’t see this brought up in the news a lot. 
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder what is the reason for the banning of books. I also wonder what makes it so a book gets banned. Who decides what books get banned? Why have some states not banned books yet?
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because my state has banned 11-100 books. It’s crazy to think that there is a possibility that some books that I have read in school may be banned.
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    Fifty shades of banned.

raw_comment:
What appears at the top of the article is not a graph. 
    
    It is a map: a choropleth map, to be specific: a powerful tool that allows those reading it to discern regional patterns, or the lack of them, in the variable being mapped. 
    
    We see them every election night, when we watch as states flip from some neutral tone to red or blue, showing a Reblican or a Democratic victory in that state  Did you ever once hear the even most ill-informed of election night pundits refer to those maps as graphs?
    
    Any data collected on a state-by-state basis can be mapped the same way: ditto data collected county by county, district by district, country by country, etc. Commonly a range of dark to light tones of a single color distinguishes places with higher to lower unemployment rates, or numbers of millionaires per 100,000 residents, or mean family income. The number of different datasets that can be mapped this way is essentially limitlesss. 
    
    The ease of grasping data mapped this way is striking. Now think of the same data on a bar graph. No meaningful relationships can pop out that way. When New Jersey and New York share similar data values on a map, it's not as conspicuous as when New York and New Mexico do. The question, "Why?" arises, followed by several others. That's a launching pad for critical thinking. We need all the critical thinking we can get.
    
    Next lesson: Greenland is WAY smaller than Africa, despite what some maps seem to show. Please alert Mr. Trump.

raw_comment:
Many readers have commented that Florida and Texas have banned so many books and wondered why.
    Governer Ron DeSantis (R-FL) and Governor Greg Abbott (R-TX) have been very proactive about banning books they believe are harmful for children to read. 
    Florida was once a heavily Democratic state but has consistently become majority Republican in recent years due to the influx of Republicans relocating from "Blue" states like NY and California to escape high taxes, harsh NY winters, traffic, fires, earthquakes, and Democratic policies with which they disagree.
    There are some areas in Florida that are still somewhat less conservative like SE Fla, parts of Central and NE Fla but in the last few years it has turned into a "Red" state and the majority of voters elect more conservative politicians who have banned certain books from public schools.
    I am not at all surprised that Florida seems to be a leader in this movement having observed the changing demographics in the state in recent years.

raw_comment:
" Erasing Education: The impact of Book Bans on Student Learning"
    What do you notice?
    The graph highlights the number of banned books across the U.S. from July to December 2023. Texas has the most, with over 3,000 bans, followed by Florida and other southern states with big numbers. While many states have fewer than 100 or none at all. 
    What do you wonder?
    Why are some states, like Texas and Florida, banning significantly more books than other states? What kind of books are being banned, and who decides.
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    Book bans impact education and access to information, which affects students ability to engage with diverse ideas. This raises questions about how decisions might influence learning in my community.

    I’m curious about why those five states have banned little to no books at the school level as well as why some states have banned 10 or more books. Did people have problems with the book and had it banned completely from the school board or was this a safety issue? 
    This relates to my community because few books are banned in the state but I wonder if those books were genuinely a problem if it was unsuited for people in the school district to read or if it was unsafe in general.
     A catchphrase could be: “Book Bans Across the States: Why Some Schools Say No to Certain Reads” This graph helps give a visual representation of books banned in each state. It shows which states have stricter bans and which have fewer, this helps us understand where and maybe even why certain books are restricted.

raw_comment:
The Restriction of Speech
    The graph, sourced by Pen America, makes it almost impossible not to wonder: what is being kept from me, and what should we keep from our youth? With such a progressive movement of silencing and removing works from states, it's easy to get lost in knowing what is right or wrong. Are these books being banned because they are bad and hurting the minds of our youth or are they being banned to push an agenda? Should Americans be letting their children read books that fill their minds with wrong things? This graph shows Florida, having Texas close behind, banning the most books. On the other hand, states like Alaska, Hawaii, Arizona, Montana, Alabama, and Nevada have no books banned. Any book can be in any of the states, so that raises the worry of why books are banned in some places and not others. When viewing this topic from the American standpoint you can stand to reason the fight for our First Amendment: the Freedom of Speech. Americans must also push to fight to keep books that may be indoctrinating youths off the shelf. Americans should have raised concerns about this drastic variety of 0 books to 6,000 being banned, so go to a local library or school board meeting to voice your concerns. This choice by states can lead to either our youth's safety or the chance of a fight regarding the want to protect one's freedoms. The choices are up to the avid reader in each state, which depending on where you are, may limit what you can access.

    I noticed that Texas and Florida have the most banned books. I kind of expected Texas but not Florida, so I wonder why they have so many. Additionally, this subject causes me to wonder why books are banned to begin with. If the nature of the book isn't compatible with someone why don't they just pick a different book to read? I guess it depends on how bad the book is but I'm not sure. I also wonder if parents play a big role in books getting banned. This relates to me and my community because I live in the United States specifically in Texas. The banning of books can negatively affect peoples education on certain topics.

raw_comment: The graph shows that book bans aren’t just a Southern issue since both the North and South have states with over 500 banned books. Florida and Texas have the most bans, which could be because some adults might lack understanding or be intolerant of certain topics. This connects to my experience in Texas, where I’ve seen adults react negatively to “sensitive” topics they think kids shouldn’t learn about. A good title for this graph could be “Book Bans: Intolerance or Intelligence?” because it makes people think about why books are being banned.

raw_comment:
I notice on this graph that Texas and Florida are the two most prominent states that ban books. I wonder if the history of each state has something to do with how many books get banned. I also wonder if politics has anything to do with the amount of banned books. After looking at the map of the most recent election, I noticed that a lot of the states that ban more books tend to be red states. This makes me wonder if politics has a role in this issue. This relates to me and my community because we live in Texas, which is a top state in the number banned books. I have been through majority of high school and have been through courses taking these banned books into consideration. Last year, we spent a good part of both the first and second semester learning and reading books that have been banned. There was a big focus on these books in particular for me and my community because they were banned.

raw_comment:
Unbalanced Book Ban Throughout the United States
    I notice that most of the states on the map have at least one banned book, with a few exceptions. I found it interesting that Florida has banned so many books in the educational system, yet many other states have banned only a few and seem to be getting by just fine. I wonder why Florida banned so many books. If other states have the same books in school libraries, why aren’t they banned as well? I’m curious if the banning of books in certain states depends on their state history, as some banned books may reflect negative events of certain states. This graph suggests that the state I live in hasn’t banned many books. The community I live in has the ability to read almost all available books. This could be directly effecting educational systems, as it allows students to read nearly anything available in school libraries. This article makes me more aware of the books held in my school library and in other school libraries.

raw_comment:
Are banned books beneficial?
    I noticed that the states with the most banned books are Texas and Florida by quite a bit. Most states are in the 10 to 300 range but these states are in the 3,000 to 6,000 range which is a lot. This has much to do with their population community and school system choices. I wonder what types of books are being banned. And why do Texas and Florida have the most banned books, if it was just because of the population then California should also be up there with a lot being banned. This relates to my community because I live in Colorado and Colorado is on the graph. We also have a library at our school and I think that if books are being banned we should know what they are and the reasoning behind it.

raw_comment: Analyzing this map I initially noticed the huge amount of books that were banned and I originally had no idea that so many books were banned in the United States. There also seem to be more books banned on the eastern side. I also thought about what could cause so many bans on books, especially in Texas and Florida. How are they banning thousands of books while other states aren’t banning any? It also came to mind what could have caused such a huge amount of books to be banned so recently. Why are there states banning so many books now? There was a huge jump in the number of books that were banned from 2022 to 2023 (about 9,000 or more). But what could be the cause of this? Could it be historical, political, or maybe even cultural reasons why Texas and Florida have banned so many while other states like Nevada haven’t banned any? I feel like there would have to be a huge number of people in Texas and Florida who thought certain books were bad or had sensitive material to cause the banning of so many books while many other states didn’t seem to have those kinds of problems.

raw_comment: After thoroughly looking into this graph, I noticed it displays information about banned books at a state level from July to December 2023. I noted that Texas and Florida had the highest number of banned books, in contrast to states with zero banned books, such as Hawaii, Nevada, New Mexico, Montana, and Alabama. This struck me as odd since a few states are in similar areas, so it’s not necessarily a contrast in location. The majority of states, however, have less than 500 banned books, which is still a lot, considering how much effort and time is put into writing a novel. This makes me wonder what content has to be in a book for it to get banned? How is it decided that documented literature can be taken away from new generations? In my freshman year, we read To Kill A Mockingbird, which is seen as controversial due to its racist language and themes. After reading this book, I felt educated on what that time period was like. It gave me and my classmates a new perspective on how people were treated then. This grasp on a previous period in human history enlightened me and showed me how different we are as a society today. raw_comment:
Hiding Knowledge From Future Generations
    I notice that only eight out of the fifty states have no banned books in their scholastic libraries. This is a shockingly small number of states that give their students complete access to any books they may want to read or research. My question is, why are some states restricting access to certain books? Is it because of their controversial topics? Some of the books banned in these states are historical books that give you background knowledge about the past that is less talked about. For example, Uncle Tom’s Cabin is banned in many Southern states and their schools because of its controversial topic of slavery. I acknowledge that some books express sensitive content that school districts don’t want their kids to learn, but almost every single piece of literature should be available to young students who are learning about the past, present, and future of the world they live in. Every piece of literature ever written is or will be a part of documented history, and it isn’t right to deny future generations this history or knowledge, no matter how controversial it is.

raw_comment:
I notice that there isn't any correlation between culture and the books banned and it may have more to do with history or possibly no correlation at all. The two biggest states with the most bans are Texas and Florida which are both southern states that are very populous which could have some meaning as to why the books are heavily banned. As you look across the states, no noticeable pattern occurs and it seems scattered into many states that have no connections in almost any way. This is shown as a state like Pennsylvania has a large amount of heavily banned books, but every single neighboring state is not as bad: this is shown in the other heavily banned states like Wisconsin, Texas, and Florida all have little to no banned books in surrounding states. It makes you wonder why these states specifically are very “sensitive” or find the books offensive and inappropriate. I think the reason could range from generally just the political party and the decision makers of the state to possibly history or the culture or “type of people” in the state. This could track back to me or almost any student as it could limit or censor the types of content available in books and could halt the information needed to learn.
    "The Censorship of Literature"

Looking at the graph, I noticed that Flordia has the highest number of books banned overall.  After Flordia, Texas is coming in with a strong second. A number as high as 10,046 for banned books in the United States is an overwhelming number even to consider.  There are 8 states that I have noticed that have decided not to ban books.  One of those states is located in the south and is the only southern state not to have banned books.  Looking at all these overarching numbers, I wonder why people even choose to ban books.  Yes, there may be some things in books that some people shouldn’t read, but that is based on maturity.  If people can handle it and some people can’t, it shouldn’t be taken away from the people who can.  Now, also knowing Flordia has the highest amount of banned books, I wonder why that is.  Are books being banned because of government views- Republican and Democratic states?  Living in Colorado, I also wonder what 1-10 books are banned here.  In my high school career, we have read many books.  Not only in school but also throughout my life.  Books have been a large perspective holder for me to fully grasp and understand things as a whole.  For example, reading books has taught me strong meanings of ways people should be treated.  More so, books have also helped me understand words (definitions) as a whole to help me gain a strong connection to the world and everyday spoken criteria.
    "Goodbye Knowledge, Hello Google."

raw_comment:
What’s Left to Read?
    I noticed that almost all states in America have banned at least one book. This is very controversial regarding the idea of freedom of speech and all the protections America has for that. I also noted that the more southeastern states had higher amounts of books banned, especially Florida and Texas. I wonder why there is such a high amount of book banning there rather than in states further north. I also wonder if there is a universal book that is banned in the majority of these states. In all, this relates to me as a student since books are being banned in schools. Although Colorado was on the lower end of the spectrum in this graph, that does not mean it always will be. Which begs even more questions, such as: “What books Colorado has already banned?”, “Will more be banned?”, “What dictates that a book should be banned?”, “Can it be stopped?”, and so on.

raw_comment: One thing that I noticed about this graph was the outliers of Florida and Texas. This made me wonder why there was a disproportionate amount of banned books in these states compared to states that didn't ban book bans like Illinois. I also wonder what makes content bannable in Texas or Florida but not bannable in other states. Also, are the books more about their history or more fiction-based? This subject connects to me and my community because specific books that feature violence, politics, or religion are not put out for everybody to use. This small amount of censorship allowed for work and school environments to feel safer without having the pressure of these topics forced down your throat by some people. Although the books are not “banned” they are certainly looked down upon in the public eye. If I were to make a headline I would probably make it, “ A Plague of Book Banning.”

raw_comment: First of all, the graph shows that most states have districts with banned books. It seems as though the vast majority of states fall under the “1-10” and “11-100” banned books categories. However, the only states with at least 1,001 banned books are Texas and Florida. This makes me wonder: is there a correlation between the number of banned books in a state and their political views? Which district officials, and particularly how many, are responsible for banning books? Do they accurately represent the voices of stakeholders, including teachers and parents? If not, this could demonstrate oligarchical corruption in our democratically driven communities. And perhaps most obviously, is the practice of banning books generally effective in protecting the education of students? If not, we must evaluate to what extent book banning negatively affects education. Because I personally believe book banning is a negative practice, I would name the graph “Book Banning: Dangerously Restrictive Education.”

The main idea is that the ideals told in the books are too much for children to handle and children should not read them. This relates to my community because my local library chooses to not display books covering sensitive topics such as religion, and violence and other sensitive topics. raw_comment: I notice in this graph that this information is from a very short period of time (July-December) in 2023. It is interesting that some states, such as Florida and Texas are in the dark red, indicating a high amount of banned literature, while some states have banned 0 books during this period. The dark red indicates numbers of over 3,000 books being banned in just a few months. This is very shocking and makes you wonder what qualities these works retain that creates so much controversy to the point where it needs to be completely censored from the public. I wonder if the content of these banned books is directly based on the political opinions of the state. Is it really ethical to ban books if our first amendment right–protecting our freedom of speech–is prevalent, perhaps today more than ever? This connects to my community personally because I think reading classic literature is very important, however, classic works that we have read in previous years at school are being challenged as being of controversial nature. These works include Of Mice and Men, and To Kill a Mockingjay, which both portray important themes about our society  that cannot simply be overlooked because they contain sensitive topics. I think it is important to not shield important messages from children in schools due to controversy because controversy in our world and country is unavoidable. “Should Literature be Censored in America?”

raw_comment:
The banning of books throughout the states is not equal, with outliers such as Texas and Florida having many more books banned than others. Likewise, other outliers include the states with no such books banned: Nevada, Montana, Arizona, etc. This leads me to question whether these states have any corresponding historical positions that would explain their legislation concerning books. For example, Texas and Florida have recent historical tendencies to be more conservative, as opposed to states that haven't banned any books leaning more on the democratic side. All of these are affected by factors such as culture, economics, and physical location. As students' this has a direct effect on the type of content that we are allowed to read as of right now, and possibly even in the future depending on whether or not there is some type of pattern. Looking at the environment within our school district and the student population itself, the general consensus concerning the banning of books would probably be discomfort regardless of whether or not they were actually being read. The people in this area of Colorado I feel are very expressive and like the ability to read or do whatever they want, so something like this would probably be disliked by the masses.
    "Books Increasing U.S Division"

raw_comment:
The banning of books throughout the states are not equal, with outliers such as Texas and Florida clearly having many more books banned than others. Likewise, other outliers include the states with no such books banned: Nevada, Montana, Arizona, etc. This leads me to question whether these states have any corresponding historical positions that might have lead their legislation concerning books. For example, Texas and Florida have recent historical tendencies to be more conservative, as opposed to states that havent banned any books leaning more to the democratic side. All of these are affected by factures such as culture, economics, and physical location. As students this has a direct effect on the type of content that we are allowed to read as of right now, and possibly even in the future depending on whether or not there is some type of pattern. Looking at the environment within our school district and the student population itself, the general consensus concerning the banning of books would probably be discomfort regardless of whether or not they were actually being read. The people in this area of Colorado I feel are very expressive and like the ability to read or do whatever they want, so something like this would probably be disliked by the masses.
    "Reading Works Is a Right, Not to Be Taken Away By The State"

Title: A reader's nightmare
    I notice that on the east side of the United State, there are more states that banned books than the west. This makes me wonder how the opposing sides would differ in terms of intelligence and personality because one side is being with-held knowledge more than the other. This relates to my community and I because we are from Texas, which is the second state that has the most banned books. I've heard many things that people categorize Texas as and I feel that our staggering amounts of banned books could contribute to it.

raw_comment:
The main thing I noticed was Florida's dark red color. I've read about the Florida "book bans", and I agree with them. I think the term "book bans" is inaccurate, because the books are not banned. They are simply removed from a school. If a student wanted to read a book, he or she could either check it out from a library, or order it off Amazon. Most of the books Florida has removed contained pornography, and I say good riddance to bad rubbish!
    
    I think that, beyond removing pornography and age inappropriate content, book removal should be voted on by parents of the school's students. Parents should know and be able to choose what their children can read.

raw_comment: After analyzing the graph I noticed that this data is from July to December 2023 and depicts the number of banned books per state. Florida has the highest number of books banned from around 3,0001 to 6,000 and Texas is close behind with 1,001 to 3,000. States like Arizona, Nevada, Montana, Alabama, and Hawaii have around zero. The graph depicts that typically Southeastern states seem to have more states that banned over 1 to 10 books and Northwestern states typically have a lower average. By looking at this graph it makes me wonder why books are banned and who decided what to ban. This makes me curious as to whether there are similar topics discussed in most banned books. Do different states' politics influence what books can and can't be outlawed? For example, are majority-ruled Republican states less likely to have prohibited books or the other way around? Is the government trying to hide to Americans certain subjects discussed in books and if so why? In my freshman honors English class, we read two books that are often banned in the US: To Kill a Mockingbird and Of Mice and Men. Both books described the hardships faced at that time and allowed me to gain perspective on these periods. Without the books, it would be hard to understand certain points the author made stand out about racism, sexism, and other sensitive subjects. However, sometimes the author of the book can be seen as insensitive and can personally hurt certain individuals views.

raw_comment: After looking at the graph I noticed a few different things. The first thing I noticed were the seven states within the country that don’t have banned books: Arizona, Nevada, Montana, Hawaii, Connecticut, Alabama, and Delaware. I also noticed that the map is solely of the United States. Another observation I had was that Florida and Texas have the most banned books in the whole country. This makes me wonder what types of books are banned in Colorado and why they are even banned at all. I wonder what the constraints are of banned books are and what steps are taken to get a book banned in the state and why a book would even be bad enough to ban when you have the choice to read a book in the first place. This connects to me because I know that I have read banned books before within the state of Colorado, so what does it mean when a book is “banned” if students still have access to it. Not only this, but this connects to my community because how are books banned in schools supposed to be segregated from non-banned books in the community library because you can access them through your local library and then bring them on campus without ever knowing that book was banned. It also sparks the thought that many teachers or even administrators don’t know the list of banned books by memory, so how are they supposed to enforce it? A catchy headline that captures the graphs main idea is America’s Book Ban Battle of 2023: Which States Are Leading the Crackdown?

raw_comment:
Limitation of Learning
    In this graph, I immediately noticed that Texas and Florida are the states with the largest number of banned books. I wonder how 5 states have absolutely zero books banned when some novels cover very harsh or graphic subjects. This graph relates to my community because I live in Texas, and there are many books that students like myself are not permitted to read today. For example, in my English class last year every student did research on a book that was banned in another area and gave their opinion on if they agreed that it should be banned or not, and many disagreed. Therefore, there were enough books for all students to research while still having a few options left over, which can limit students' knowledge.

raw_comment: I noticed a few things. The first is that there are only 7 states in the entire country that don’t have any banned books. I also noticed that in Florida and Texas there are the most amount of banned books. I notice this is a map solely of  the U.S and that the information is from 2023. I can see specifically in Colorado, where I live, that there really aren’t that many banned books here. This makes me wonder what books are banned in my state, and if I have ever read them. I also wonder why in Texas and Florida there is such a vast amount of banned books. Is it a politically related problem? This graph also makes me wonder why I don’t really see any patterns. Throughout the entire country, different numbers of banned books exist. For instance, although Alabama is between two states with banned books, and in a close proximity to Florida which has the most, it still remains with zero banned books. I'm curious as to who is deciding what books to ban and what exactly does a banned book even mean. Is it just banned from schools or can you not purchase it in that state? This relates to me and my community because throughout my highschool experience we've been required to read numerous banned books. This makes me wonder what banned even means if I read them in school. It also relates to me because I do love reading and I would hope that my favorite books don’t get banned. A catchy title for this graph could be “The U.S distribution of banned books.”

I notice that the major red states on the map (with the most banned books; 3,001-6,000), are Texas and California. I also noticed that there are 8 grey states, which means there are no books banned in those states. I wonder why Texas and Florida have the most books banned, and if it has anything to do with the fact that they are big republican states. In other words, I wonder if politics have anything to do with the book ban by states. I wonder what specific books are being banned by these states... is there a specific pattern with the types of books that are being banned across the country? I would be curious to find out what type of books are banned in NJ. I would say these numbers really impact those states such as Texas and Florida, where several thousands of books are banned. I wonder if this limits their access to gain information on specific topics.

This makes me wonder if the banning of books has more to do with county legislation or state legislation and who should hold the final say. Since only 1-10 books have been banned in Colorado, it does not impact me as much as it would impact a student living in Florida or Texas.

raw_comment:
I noticed that Florida has banned the most books, at 3,001-6,000, with Texas falling shortly behind at 1,001 to 3,000.  I also noticed that Hawaii, Alaska, Montana, Nevada, Arizona, Alabama, Connecticut, and Delaware have not banned any books.  These states vary with population, education, and political standing, so I wonder why they have not been swayed by the banning of books.  I noticed that the majority of the West Coast has banned little books, while the East Coast has a mix of states that have banned smaller numbers of books and larger numbers of books.  I also wonder what caused Florida and Texas to have banned so many books, and who exactly banned the books.  I wonder what kind of content the books have for them to be nationally banned.  This relates to me and my community because New Jersey is a state in which 1-10 books have been banned.  I have also read a few of the books on the banned books list, relating directly to me.
    Headline: "Turning a New Page: A State to State Ban of Books"

Headline- Off the Shelves: 2023 Book Banning Wave
    What do I notice?  
    I noticed that Texas and Florida are the states with the most banned books. On the other hand, Alabama, Nevada, Arizona, and Montana have 0 banned books. 
    What do I wonder? 
    I wonder if Texas and Florida being namely Republican states has anything to do with them banning books. I also wonder why they are banning 3,001 - 6000 while some states that are also Republican are banning 500 or less books.  I also wonder what the criteria has to be for a book to be banned and who decides when a book should be banned?
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This connects to my community because because I live in a state with 1-10 banned books. As a high school student, I am constantly reading books and using them to enhance my learning. Books that are that are part of my school curriculum could be banned in the future.

1. After looking at the graph, I noticed that it compares the number of banned books in each state at the school district level from July through December of 2023. The state with the most banned books is Florida, with between 3,001 and 6,000 banned books. raw_comment:
Headline: A Book Ban Wave Across the Nation
    The graph depicts a map of the United States. The states are colored based on how many books are banned in each state. One thing I noticed is that Florida is the darkest state. This means that from July to December 2023, 3,001-6,00 books were banned. Texas is trailing behind as being the second darkest, with 1,001-3,000 books prohibited. I wonder if these two states, being mostly made up of Republicans, has an effect on the number of books banned. This affects me because I live in New Jersey, and there are only 1-10 books banned.

raw_comment:
I noticed that only a handful of states hadn't banned any books; seven out of fifty states had zero documented banned books. Why did so many states ban these books? Why does Florida have the most banned books? Why do only six states have no banned books? I wonder what makes a book able to be banned, and why so many of them are. Since I live in Texas, this graph is interesting to me because I didn't completely grasp how many books were actually banned in the state. How much am I truly missing out on when it comes to literature?
    
    A good headline for this graph would be: "Bans on Literature: A Comparison Between States"

raw_comment:
1. After looking at the graph, I noticed that it compares the number of banned books in each state at the school district level from July through December of 2023. The state with the most banned books is Florida, with between 3,001 and 6,000 banned books. The states with the least number of banned books are Montana, Nevada, Arizona, Alabama, Delaware, and Connecticut. These states have no banned books. The remaining states have between 1 and 3,000 banned books. 
    2. After looking at the graph, I wonder why so many books are banned. Do school districts have a voice in banned books? Why is there such a large range of banned books? Why are books banned in some states but not others? How do parents and teachers react to books being banned in school districts? Should books be banned at all?  
    3. This relates to my community because in school, we read books that are commonly banned. Also, books that are currently part of school curriculums could be banned in the future. This impacts what schools teach and what students learn at school. 
    4. A headline for this graph is “Are Banned Books Bad?”

raw_comment:
This graph shows that most states have banned books, but very few have a banned book count over five hundred. In the past few years, book bans have been a very hot topic, leading to heated discourse about where or if a line should be drawn regarding the content of a book. I noticed that notoriously blue states have little to no banned books. On the other hand, notoriously red states, specifically Texas and Florida, have over one thousand books banned. I wonder why the range of banned books is so vast in Florida and Texas. It seems like it would be easier to simply have more precise data. I also wonder if this graph includes books that are challenged in certain areas. This relates to my community because, as a high school student, I like to be aware of the books that are restricted in my area and others.

raw_comment:
This graph shows the amount of books banned per state. I noticed that the states with the most banned books are Texas and Florida. People ban books when they don't want certain information to grow in the minds of the people. Banned books usually have more progressive themes that are perceived as threatening to the control of politicians. It makes sense that Texas and Florida have the most banned books because those states are some of the most conservative in the country and they may feel threatened by the more progressive messages featured in these books. I wonder what the process is for banning books. This impacts my community because the books that we read in school could be banned in the future. 
    Headline: Books On Fire

raw_comment:
The first thing that caught my eye when analyzing the graph was that this data was taken from July to December 2023. I also saw that 8 of the 50 states have 0 books banned. I noticed that the darker the color, the more books are banned within the state. Furthermore, both Texas and Florida have the most banned books sitting between 1,001-3,000 and 3,001-6,000 books. 
    I wonder, since I previously mentioned the data was from 2023, how the graph would look like for 2024. Would there me any drastic changes? The note says that it does not include banned books by public libraries- what would this graph look like? What is the purpose of banning a book in school if a child can access it outside of it? Doesn't the concept of banning books violate the author's First Amendment rights?
    This relates to me and my community because I'm a high school student in a state that has 1-10 banned books, though I am grateful it isn't more. Banning books restricts people from being exposed to new things and ideas, especially in a time that is so important for developing their own thoughts and opinions. Not only this, but many books I have both read and loved, in school and out, currently are on a banned book list whether it be in my state or another's.  
    Title: "Silenced Pages, Lost in Politics: Banned Books in the States"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I noticed that the graph shows how many books have been banned in each state depending on the color. Five states have zero books banned. It seems to be pretty random. However, states in the midwest tend to ban more books. Texas and Floria have banned the most books. Banning books has dramatically increased since the pandemic. 
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder what makes certain states ban books. What makes a book up for banning? Is the decision entirely up to politicians? Or does the public have a say? 
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to my community because because I live in New Jersey. New Jersey is an area with very little book banning. So I am fortunate to live in a state that has light banning. 
    Headline - Banning is Spreading!

raw_comment:
This graph displays the number of books banned throughout the country. I noticed two things, the first being that only seven states have not banned any books other than that, every other state has at least one book banned. Second, Texas and Florida are the states that have banned the most amount of books in the US. I mainly wonder why these two states have so many banned and what is the criteria for banning books(does it differ per state?). I am also curious whether book banning has any correlation to the state's political affiliation. Finally, I am curious about how this is or is not an infringement on our First Amendment right to the freedom of speech. This is something extremely important to me because I live in a state where books are banned, and this could impact my learning. It also makes me want to look up what the regulations of my state are for banning books.
    
    Title: Book Banning: A Battle Within Education

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I notice that the number of banned books varies greatly across states. Florida stands out with between 3,001 and 6,000 books banned represented in a dark maroon red, while states like Arizona have no banned books at all, marked in grey. Pennsylvania falls somewhere in the middle with 501 to 1,000 books banned. This suggests that while book bans aren't happening everywhere, they are particularly concentrated in states like Florida and Texas. This makes me wonder: why are Florida and Texas leading the way in banning books, and what specific criteria are being used to determine which books should be removed? How do these bans affect students’ access to diverse perspectives and the freedom to think critically? I also wonder how these book bans impact educators—are they being forced to limit their teaching materials or self-censor? In my own state, there have been only 1 to 10 banned books, which feels relatively low, but it still makes me think about the impact of censorship on access to knowledge. This issue also resonates with me because I recently wrote an essay on political courage, focusing on Congressman Jamie Raskin, who has actively opposed book bans. His argument that banning books attacks First Amendment rights and harms democracy deeply connects to the current situation. In fact, Raskin’s own book was banned in Texas, so I’ve been aware of this issue for some time.
    
    Headline: "Book Bans Surge Nationwide, with Florida and Texas Leading the Charge"

raw_comment: To Ban or Set Free: I notice how Texas and Florida are the main states that have the most banned books in their own districts. I wonder what books the districts are banning and why they are being banned. I feel that majority of the books that are being banned are because of the content in the books. This relates to myself and my community because last year in my English class, the teacher was telling the class about our district in Texas wanting to ban some books that we have read. We even had a project about the banned books. Each student had a different book in each class and the point was to read it and give our thoughts on if it were to be banned or not. The books the students got to choose were books banned in places other than Texas, so if they were to be banned in Texas, then the project would have to be changed.

raw_comment:
The first thing my eyes were drawn to was the two states Texas and Florida because of how drastically red they are in comparison to the other states. Florida and Texas are two large southern states, both seen as "red" states because of how they fall politically, which is Republican. Knowing that both these states are largely Republican makes me wonder if that might affect why they have the most banned books. As a student who lives and goes to school in Texas the large amount of banned books in my state affects me drastically because it hinders me from reading and having access to books that have a subject matter that the politicians that are in charge of banning books deem as to 'taboo'. 
    title-  Books lost to time and politics

raw_comment:
I noticed that there are a lot of states that haven't banned any books. I noticed that Florida and Texas have the most banned books. I saw that the number of books banned is mostly over 100. There are many things I wonder about when I look at this graph, one being the types of books that are banned. What causes a book to be banned? Is there a more "bannable" genre? Are books like allegory, satire, or non-fiction novels (The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins or 1984 by George Orwell) more likely to be banned than other books? What is the purpose of withholding literature from children when they can access and read outside of school and public libraries? Is banning books an infringement of the author's First Amendment right? This impacts my community and me because restricting books can impair the public's access to literature. I am lucky to live in a state where the number of banned books is 1-10 and not over 100. I love so many books that I love, and many are currently on a banned list in other states. 
    Title: The Censorship Chronicles: Banned books per state!

raw_comment:
In this graph, it displays the amount of books banned in each state by color. The white means that no books are banned and dark red has 3001-6000 books banned. As the colors get darker, more books are banned. I notice that Texas and Florida have the most amount of books banned, while around six states have no books banned. I wonder if people think that banning books violates the First Amendment, freedom of speech and press. Everyone should be able to express themselves, but by banning what one says, it could be argued that this violates the First Amendment rights. This relates to my community because I live in the United States and there are around 1-10 books banned. 
    The Rise of Book Banning Across The States: A Growing Restriction on Education

raw_comment:
States in the midwest, plus Florida and Texas, tend to ban more books. Not much research is required to quickly determine that this is because these states in particular have a habit of restricting education, especially education relating to diversity (such as LGBTQ+ identities or cultural diversity).
         Some things that this makes me wonder are what kind of books are banned in the smaller states outside of the midwest, and what kind of books are bad enough to be able to be banned in the states with only 1-10 banned books? It's a pretty exclusive club for those states, and I wonder the prerequisites to get in.
         While brainstorming headlines, I came up with "countless books banned throughout U.S.; children's education falters." While it's a little dramatic, it describes the situation decently. And as all good journalists know, sensationalizing it will make people read it.
         I live in Vermont, so I did some research about the books banned in Vermont. It's one of those states that has very few books banned in it. I couldn't find any sources that told me which books were banned exactly, but knowing Vermont, I believe they're books that are especially against equity or diversity, and/or directly promote violence against these groups, though that's a guess.

raw_comment:
Book Banning in the U.S.: A Prominent Occurrence
    In this graph, I notice that almost every state has at least 1-10 books banned. There are only six states that do not have any bans. I also noticed that Texas and Florida have the most book bans. It is a general trend that Republican-lean states tend to have more bans on books. Most democratic-leaning states still have book bans, just not as much. Because the data from this graph was collected in 2023, I wonder if it is outdated. I wonder if, in the past 1-2 years, there have been any major changes regarding book bans. I think this graph is trying to explain the severity of book banning as it now affects our country. The graph also tries to show us the differences between each state. This graph relates to my community because I live in New Jersey. New Jersey is an area with very little book banning. I think that banning some books is necessary for extreme cases. However, it should mainly try to be avoided, or else it contradicts freedom of speech and liberty. Therefore, my community and I should be grateful to live in New Jersey.

There are only six states that do not have any bans.
Texas and Florida have the most book bans.
It is a general trend that Republican-lean states tend to have more bans on books.
Most democratic-leaning states still have book bans.
Most democratic-leaning states do not have as many book bans as Republican-lean states.
Because the data from this graph was collected in 2023, I wonder if it is outdated.
I wonder if there have been any major changes regarding book bans in the past 1-2 years.
I think this graph is trying to explain the severity of book banning.
Book banning now affects our country.
The graph also tries to show us the differences between each state.
This graph relates to my community.
I live in New Jersey.
New Jersey is an area with very little book banning.
I think that banning some books is necessary for extreme cases.
However, banning some books should mainly be avoided.
If banning some books is not avoided, it contradicts freedom of speech and liberty.
My community and I should be grateful to live in New Jersey.

raw_comment: This graph shows the number of banned books in each state from July to December 2023. Firstly, I noticed that about only 7 states did not ban any books while Florida banned the most books closely followed by Texas. I wonder what factors led the states to ban books. Since the books are banned in both Conservative and Liberal states, it cannot be assumed that the main political party behind the state is the driving force. I also wonder why Florida and Texas banned the most books and what issues with the novels drove them to be banned. This relates to my community and myself because it shows what each state deems “inappropriate” in book material and plot. It also shows me how critical some states are with banning books and how they have a very broad spectrum of what is considered an unsuitable book that needs to be banned. A title could be “The Battle of Books.”

1. What do you notice?
    Observe that eight states, Connecticut, Delaware, Montana, Nevada, Arizona, and Alabama report no banned books. However, this data only spans a few months in 2023, which might be misleading. The absence of bans during this period doesn’t necessarily mean these states have never banned books; it could simply reflect a lack of bans within the timeframe of the study.
    2. What do you wonder?
    This raises questions about the context of these "0 cases." Are they based solely on the data collection period, or do they indicate a complete absence of bans historically? Furthermore, what constitutes a book ban? Does it require action at the state level, or could it involve decisions made by other entities, such as school districts or individual institutions?
    3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
    ​​In North Carolina, the data shows between 11 and 100 banned books—a notably broad range. This could suggest uncertainty or variability in reporting. In public schools, however, these decisions may be influenced by school districts, local authorities, or state governments. Given North Carolina's diversity, I wonder if a rising number of book bans might exacerbate tensions across communities.
    4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
    Academic Apprehension: Unpacking the Wave of Book Bans in the US

I noticed that majority of the states had at least one banned book. Meaning, more states had banned books than those without. 
          Because of this, I wondered if there was a book that was banned in majority of the states, even the ones that only had 1-10 books banned. It would be interesting to see a list of book titles that were banned in certain states. 
           What would have been different about the data if collected by 
    different people or in a different time period?

I also imagine that the people who collected the data chose to display it in a scale format (eg. 1-10), whereas some people probably would have selected specific counties to represent each state- thus, skewing the overall state data. 
          Catchy headline: America: The Land of Literature Laws

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I noticed that numerous states have zero books banned, which is a stark contrast to the states where there are over 3000 books banned. I also noticed that they used a darker color red to show more books banned, which associated red with a more restrictive behavior. 
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder at what level are books banned at, do they ban at the state, local, or federal level? Is there a correlation between political views and the number of banned books per state?
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    My community is shown on the graph, in North Carolina, and also I go to a school that is private, so maybe book bans wouldn’t affect me in my community. I also have access to a lot of banned books through online use, which means these things don’t apply to me. 
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    State Lines and Federal Crimes: Banned Books Across the USA

raw_comment:
We notice that few states have zero book bans, and some of them (Alabama, Montana) are, surprisingly, in more conservative states. Though the eastern and southern states tend to have a higher number of books banned compared to western states, Texas and Florida have the highest number of banned books. We notice that Illinois and Minnesota have some banned books, even though banning books is supposedly banned. Also, we notice that our state of Wisconsin has a relatively large number of banned books. 
    
    We wonder what are the main topics of the books that are banned. We wonder why some states have more banned books than others. We also wonder what book banning looks like in the rest of the world. Additionally, we want to know why book banning increased after the pandemic? We want to know what the per capita number of books banned is for each state.
    
    This graph relates to us as high school students in a state (Wisconsin) that has a relatively high number of banned books. We wonder if our access to knowledge is limited due to these bans. 
    
    Catchy title: Blank Pages: Book Banning Throughout the United States

raw_comment:
I notice that there seem to be 8 states with no books banned, and those are Connecticut, Delaware, Montana, Nevada, Arizona, and Alabama. I also notice that this data is over the course of a few months in 2023, which could be misleading as the 0s could be that those books just didn't ban any books during that period (not necessarily that they've never banned any books).
    
    I wonder if these 0 cases are referring to over the course of the data collection, or if they're referring to of all time. Either way, what qualifies a book ban, and does it have to be by state, or could there be other kinds of bans? 
    
    In North Carolina, it seems there are 11-100 books banned. That's a wide range, and maybe it's because there's some uncertainty. Because I go to a private school, our school is able to decide what books are appropriate for us to engage with. At public schools, this regulation may not be up to the schools, and could be up to a school district, local, or state government. Because North Carolina is such a diverse state, I wonder if ongoing and increasing amounts of book bans could create tension. 
    
    Headline: Academic Apprehension: Unpacking the Wave of Book Bans in the US.

raw_comment:
The scale for the number of banned books greatly differs. Florida is the only state with a very dark red color, the same as Texas and the bright red. Meanwhile, many states fall within a wide range such as 11-100 banned books. This could skew interpretations of the data by including states with 14 banned books and states with 96 banned books in the same category. 
    
    What are the differences in legislation that cause such a vast range of banned books? What allows Florida to ban so many books while states like Alabama, which I would’ve thought to have many bans, do not have any banned books? 
    
    North Carolina falls within the 11-100 banned books category. I’m curious to learn more as to what types of books are banned within the state. Are there any common trends in the content within the books? Do these book bans affect elementary, middle, or high school students? Are there certain districts within North Carolina that heavily contribute to this number? 
    
    Florida hates books! Florida leads the country in the number of banned books.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
    
    I notice that this data is only from a few months in 2023, which could be very misleading to someone who isn’t paying attention to all of the details of the graph. I also see that a handful of states didn’t ban books during the data period, but that does not mean that they have never banned books. 
    
    What do you wonder? 
    
    I wonder how this map would compare to the total number of books banned in each state. I’m also curious about why Texas and Florida feel the need to ban such a high number of books compared to the other forty-eight states. 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community? 
    
    I believe that literature is an important part of history and education (not to mention a resource I use on a daily basis), so banning books should involve a lengthy process that determines whether or not the ban is justified. Also, we’ve read a fair amount of banned books in our English classes that teach valuable lessons that other students should get to experience. 
    
    Headline: Texas and Florida Lead the Book Ban Charge In 2023

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I notice that very few states have no ban on any books. Texas and Florida have the highest number of books banned. Texas has between 1,001 and 3,000 books banned, and Florida has between 3,001 and 6,000 books banned. Most of the states have either 1-10 books banned or 11-100. The data being reported is based on book bans within school districts.
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder what the reason is for so many books needing to be banned. What is so wrong with them that they can no longer be read? Who is responsible for the banning? Is it the government? Below the graph, one paragraph states that an unknown number of books have also been removed, so I am curious about how many books that would be. Mostly, I just wonder why such a thing would happen in the first place.
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me and my community because I am a student and an avid reader. At school, a book ban could impact my curriculum and many others. In my previous classes, we’ve read books regularly that may be on the banned book list now. Books express a variety of beliefs, ideas, and stories. With the book ban, we will no longer be able to have access to them.
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    “The Book Ban: The Next Chapter of US Education?”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I noticed that there is a high majority of 1-500 books banned in most states across America. In some states, though, such as Florida, there were 3,000-6,000 books banned, with Texas close behind with 1,000-3,000 banned.
    
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why there were so many banned books in Florida. I also wonder why some states have not banned any books- are they allowed to?
    
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This affects my and my community because I am in an area that has 11-100 banned books, which I was unaware of.
    
    
    Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
    "Chapters Cut Short: The Spread of Book Bans Across America"

raw_comment:
I notice that Utah has a considerably more direct approach to banning books than most of its surrounding states, assuming states like Nevada and Arizona are just banging lower amounts of books and are not counted under this data.  I also notice that Alaska seems to have a very small amount of book bans; as does Montana.
    
    I wonder if the states shaded light gray are just not giving their input for this graph, or if they are genuinely banning so small a number of books that there is no real point in including them in the graph.

    Texas - The Lone Star State of Suppression : The Banning of Books Persists Throughout Numerous US States.

raw_comment:
- I notice that book bans seem to be more frequent in southern states, and therefore those states are also taking more stands against book banning. this dichotomy is intriguing, because southern states--typically leaning more conservative--seem to be going through a crisis of free speech, and can't collectively decide whether banning books or banning book bans aligns best with their values.
    - I wonder why Florida, of all states, bans most books. Perhaps the older traditionalists living in Florida are responsible for the book bans.
    - Michigan is just about in the middle of the book banning frequencies chart. Not too shabby, although I'd prefer it if we made like Nevada and banned book bans. Some of the books we read in school, like Catcher in the Rye, are banned in other states, so we've got that going for us.
    - Book Banning Goes South

What do you notice?
    I noticed that Florida and Texas have the most banned books. I noticed that mainly every school district on the south side has a lot of bans. Hawaii has no books banned. 
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why so many books are banned? I wonder what caused them to be banned? I also wonder why some schools are allowing some books and others are not depending on the area?
    How does this relate to you?

There are certain books that shouldn’t be read by all, but they have deep meaning behind them that helps influence different learning.

    “Banned Books Across America”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
    I noticed that most of the states have some number of books banned for the school districts. I also saw that more of the southern states have more restrictions on books for some reason, the east coast as well has many bans. 
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why some of the books have been banned? Who decides that a book has to be banned for any reason? I also wondered why some states had no book bans compared to the rest of the country?
    What relationship to the community?
    The relationship I see is that many students read books in my classes, and some may not be the best choices for those readers. Therefore, banning some of the books would allow better focus on topics the schools would want.
    Catchy headline: BBB: Bosses Banning Books?

raw_comment:
1.  What I notice are the few states that do not have book bans.  Two that I see are decidedly liberal states.  Two states have trended "purple" over the past couple of election cycles, but two are decidedly red states where you would expect some sort of book ban.  I also notice that my own state, New Mexico, which is decidedly blue, has a handful of book bans, which surprises me and makes we want to find out what they are.
    
    2.  If both red and blue states are banning books, what are the driving factors?  Are they ideological or something else?  Is there something in common in the bans in red and blue states that indicates an underlying motivation?
    
    3.  I worry that attempts to indocrinate to a particular point of view by withholding and directing reading material to children and even adults through book banning can infect any community.
    
    4.  Book Bans Transcend Politics

raw_comment:
I notice that Florida has the highest number of banned books and Texas is a close second. Also, Montana, Nevada, Arizona, Alabama, Delaware, Connecticut, Alaska, and Hawaii each have zero banned books.
    
    I wonder if these book bans result from conservative viewpoints or if the books contain truly dangerous ideas. Additionally, I wonder if the topics from banned books are also banned from being taught in schools.
    
    This relates to my community because the state I live in, New York, has 11-100 books banned. I would like to learn the reason for the book bans in my state and what topics the books were about.
    
    Headline: Censorship: States Saying Bye to Books

raw_comment:
-After looking at the graph, I noticed that Florida has the most banned books, closely followed by Texas, Wisconsin, and Pennsylvania. I also noticed that Alaska, Hawaii, Delaware, Connecticut, Alabama, Nevada, Arizona, and Montana all have 0 banned books. 
    
    -After looking at the graph, I wonder why some states have as little as zero banned books while other states have as many as 6,000 banned books. I also wonder why the books aren't being banned on a government level if some areas feel that strongly about preventing them from being read. 
    
    -This relates to me and my community because I live in New York where 11-100 books are banned. This affects me because it should be my decision what I decide to read, not my government or school district, and when that right is taken away, I should be educated so I can do something about it. Additionally, my community is affected because New York has a significant number of books banned for a state with such a high population in an area where many people feel strongly about our rights. 
    
    -A catchy headline for this graph could be "Bye Bye Books."
